description: Three same-time harmonic plots for frozen modern 10p n9: cosine displacement (a), negative-sine signed velocity (b), and negative-cosine signed acceleration (c), with the original two-cycle endpoints, eight dashed common-time guides, solid curves and axes, zeroes, positive amplitude labels, and two dashed amplitude references. All extrema, zero crossings and quarter/half-cycle phase relationships are executable. Modern English subfigure tags and semantic Latin m subscripts do not assert certainty about the original alphabet. Separate ordinate scales retain the source visual ordering and approximate amplitude proportions; they are not equal physical units. Clean analytic sampling, uniform time spacing, whitespace and label placement are justified instructional regularizations, not invented measurements. No numeric time ticks, inferred measured readings, speed-only curve, force arrows, extra cycle, science approval or promotion.

authoritativeText.text:
9. Velocity and acceleration in simple harmonic motion

When a body undergoes simple harmonic oscillation, its velocity and acceleration components along the direction of oscillation also vary harmonically with time.
The velocity component along the $OX$ axis is the first derivative of displacement $x$ with respect to time.

This component can be positive or negative;
its sign indicates the direction of motion.

Speed is the magnitude of this component and has no direction sign.
If $x=x_{\mathrm{m}}\cos\omega_0t$, then:
$v_x=x'=-\omega_0x_{\mathrm{m}}\sin\omega_0t=\omega_0x_{\mathrm{m}}\cos\left(\omega_0t+\frac{\pi}{2}\right)$ $(1.21)$

The quantity that varies harmonically here is the signed velocity component, not the always nonnegative speed.
The preceding cosine expression shows that the phase of the velocity component leads that of displacement by $\pi/2$.

When the body passes through equilibrium, its displacement is zero and its speed is greatest.
The magnitude of the velocity component is then greatest, but the component is at its positive maximum when motion is in the positive direction and at its negative minimum when motion is in the negative direction.
Not every passage through equilibrium gives the maximum signed velocity.

At either turning point, the magnitude of displacement is greatest, and both velocity and speed are zero (Figure $15$a, b).
The positive turning point gives the positive maximum displacement.

The negative turning point gives its negative minimum.
The velocity amplitude $v_{\mathrm{m}}$ is the greatest absolute value of the velocity component, or the maximum speed.

Its relation to displacement amplitude is:
$v_{\mathrm{m}}=\omega_0x_{\mathrm{m}}$.

The acceleration component along the $OX$ axis is the first derivative of the velocity component with respect to time.
From the preceding velocity expression:
$a_x=v'_x=-\omega_0^2x_{\mathrm{m}}\cos\omega_0t$,

or $a_x=\omega_0^2x_{\mathrm{m}}\cos(\omega_0t+\pi)$.
$(1.22)$

The acceleration component of simple harmonic oscillation also varies harmonically with time, with amplitude $a_{\mathrm{m}}=\omega_0^2x_{\mathrm{m}}$.
The phase difference between the acceleration component and displacement is $\pi$.
Their magnitudes reach their greatest values at the same times, but their signed maxima do not.

At the positive maximum displacement, acceleration is at its negative minimum.
At the negative minimum displacement, acceleration is at its positive maximum.
Away from equilibrium, acceleration and displacement have opposite signs, and acceleration always points toward equilibrium.

At equilibrium, both are zero.
This phase relationship is called opposition of phase (Figure $15$a, c).

Figure 15

The phase of the acceleration component leads that of the velocity component by $\pi/2$.
The relation between their amplitudes is:
$a_{\mathrm{m}}=v_{\mathrm{m}}\omega_0$.

inventory.description: Source row a: one solid rightward time axis labelled t and one solid upward quantity axis labelled X; a printed 0 sits at their origin. The row tag is a in modern English, replacing the source Cyrillic subfigure tag. Keep the positive-amplitude label xₘ; maximum uses semantic Latin m, without resolving the original subscript alphabet. No numbered time ticks, negative-amplitude labels, units, measured values, or force arrows occur. Labels are repositioned only for legibility.

Source row b: one solid rightward time axis labelled t and one solid upward quantity axis labelled vₓ; a printed 0 sits at their origin. The row tag is b in modern English, replacing the source Cyrillic subfigure tag. Keep the positive-amplitude label ω₀xₘ; maximum uses semantic Latin m, without resolving the original subscript alphabet. No numbered time ticks, negative-amplitude labels, units, measured values, or force arrows occur. Labels are repositioned only for legibility.

Source row c: one solid rightward time axis labelled t and one solid upward quantity axis labelled aₓ; a printed 0 sits at their origin. The row tag is c in modern English, replacing the source Cyrillic subfigure tag. Keep the positive-amplitude label ω₀²xₘ; maximum uses semantic Latin m, without resolving the original subscript alphabet. No numbered time ticks, negative-amplitude labels, units, measured values, or force arrows occur. Labels are repositioned only for legibility.

The original has exactly eight dashed vertical common-time guides after the solid zero-time quantity axes. They align the three plots at the successive quarter-cycle positions through the right endpoint of the second cycle. Each starts at the upper time axis, except the fourth and eighth which start at the positive displacement peaks; all continue through the lower plot to its lower reference extent. There is no ninth dashed guide at zero time, no labelled time scale, and no extension into a third cycle. Even spacing is justified by the exact harmonic phase relationships in the frozen edition, not measured scan values.

Only the velocity and acceleration plots have dashed horizontal positive-amplitude references in the source. Velocity has a dashed line from its quantity axis to the first positive velocity peak at the third common-time guide, labelled omega_0 x_m. Acceleration has a dashed line from its quantity axis to its first positive acceleration peak at the second guide, labelled omega_0 squared x_m. The displacement x_m label is at the initial positive peak without a separate dashed horizontal line. No negative-amplitude references are added.

Source a: one solid cosine displacement curve, from the positive maximum at zero time through two negative minima and the next two positive maxima, ending at the second-cycle positive maximum. Its four zero crossings align with guides 1, 3, 5, 7. Exact edition cosine regularizes scan roughness; the drawn ordinate scale is not a physical amplitude reading.

Source b: one solid negative-sine signed-velocity curve starts at zero and initially falls; it has negative minima at guides 1 and 5, positive maxima at guides 3 and 7, and zeroes at guides 2, 4, 6, 8. It is not a nonnegative speed curve. No third cycle or numerical reading is added.

Source c: one solid negative-cosine signed-acceleration curve starts at its negative minimum, peaks positively at guides 2 and 6 and negatively at guides 4 and 8; it crosses zero at guides 1, 3, 5, 7. The endpoint remains the second-cycle negative minimum; signs are opposite to displacement at common times.

Source relationships across all three rows: displacement zero coincides with a signed velocity extremum and acceleration zero; displacement extrema coincide with velocity zero and opposite-signed acceleration extrema. The frozen edition identifies velocity as cosine advanced by pi/2, acceleration advanced by pi/2 relative to velocity and pi relative to displacement. Executable signed-ordinate assertions account for the separate drawn vertical scales, rather than assuming equal physical amplitudes. Internal quarter-cycle parameters and ordinate drawing units are not printed ticks or added measured readings.
